channel.title: sgit.ai articles
channel.description: Articles and desk notes from sgit.ai, newest first.

item.title: The grant, not the prompt: a technical user believed Claude could only read his email when he asked, and in an unrelated chat it listed his inbox, the gap between mandate and reach that RiskMandate is built to close
item.description: I spent an evening with a user who is technical, a composer with a serious studio, who uses Claude chat and Claude Cowork every day. He has a scheduled task that reads a composers' forum each morning and tells him about new posts, and he connected Gmail, Calendar and his notes, clicking yes to the permissions. His expectation was clear: Claude reads his email only when he asks, in the one conversation where he asks, and the forum task never touches it. So I asked him to open an unrelated project chat and type "what emails do I have in my inbox?". Claude listed them. Nothing went wrong; that is the point. Anthropic's own documentation says a connected connector is available in every conversation and that Claude can bring it in on its own, and scheduled tasks have the same connected tools. The authority was granted when he connected Gmail, not when he typed the question. His setup also has what Simon Willison calls the lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content read every morning, and a way to send. This is the gap RiskMandate measures, the mandate (what the user expects) against the reach (what the agent can do), and the messaging we need to explain it to people who are not security specialists.

item.title: Separate Ways, explained: what my brother's synth video shows, frame by frame, and why describing work at the moment you make it is the first step to publishing it
item.description: My brother Gabriel DaCruz posted a short video of Journey's Separate Ways, played on a synthesizer in his studio and filmed from three cameras at once. Most people who watch it will not know what they are seeing. So I asked him to explain it, recorded it, and gave it to this site's agent to check and package. The explanation: a Bluetooth MIDI keyboard with no cable, a Behringer Pro-800, which is a reproduction of the Sequential Prophet-600 from 1982, chorus and delay to match the 1983 record, and, at the end, the decay turned down live so each chord goes staccato and the delay repeats the short chord. The checking found two things he had flagged himself: the record's credits list a Roland Jupiter-8, not the Prophet-5 he remembered, and his synth copies the Prophet-600, not the Prophet-5. And on the way, he mentioned, almost in passing, that he had filmed it with three old iPhones synced live to an iPad, which became an article of its own. That is the point of this one. The people who hire someone like Gabriel are the people who want to know how it was done, and the only time anyone explains it is at the moment of creation, quickly, with an agent doing the rest.

item.title: Sellable units: applying api.newsroom.sgit.ai to my brother's website, the reading meter on a composer's site that does not look like a newsroom, the pathways from a viewer to a buyer, and every lesson, score and master as something to sell
item.description: I showed my brother Gabriel the newsroom, including topping up my own reading credit, and his first question was the right one: his site should not look like a newsroom. It will not. What the newsroom's technology adds is not a look but a way to be paid: every reader starts with £5 of credit, each page uses a few pence by how much was read, a rating sets the price from nothing to double, the balance can go below zero, and a top-up through Stripe comes when the value is clear. All of it is published as an open API, api.newsroom.sgit.ai, that any page can add with a few lines. On a composer's site that looks like a composer's site, every page becomes a sellable unit: a lesson's materials, a score he owns, an analysis of what makes a song work, a how-to, a video explained, the WAVs of a piece like Amazónia. His readers are other musicians, producers and students, a demanding audience and a large one. The habit that makes it work is to create sellable units every day, at the moment of creation, and let an agent publish them. And for the works that should travel, Creative Commons Attribution with a paid licence alongside, with one honest correction: once a work is under CC BY, a buyer can get a licence on other terms, but not exclusivity.

item.title: Four iPhones and an iPad: how my brother filmed a three-camera music video with old phones synced live to Final Cut Pro, a feature Apple shipped in 2024 that he found by accident
item.description: My brother Gabriel DaCruz filmed his Separate Ways synth video from three angles at once, with no camera crew: two second-hand iPhone 12s and an iPhone 13, bought because they were cheap and he only needed the cameras, connected wirelessly to an iPad running Final Cut Pro. The iPad shows every angle live, controls each camera and records them already in sync; then he moved the project to Final Cut Pro on his Mac to finish it. The feature is Live Multicam, which Apple released in June 2024 with Final Cut Pro for iPad 2.0 and a free Final Cut Camera app. It takes up to four angles, the iPad itself can be one of them, and Apple says it works with iPhones from the XS onwards. Gabriel, who knows this world well, found it by accident and was blown away. Coverage was heavy at launch and thin since. If a working producer had not heard of it, plenty of musicians, teachers and small venues have not either. This is the setup, what it needs, and what it is good for, from interviews to a live show.

item.title: The lab that redesigned the book: how The Ultimate Insider stopped looking like a book from the 1980s, in thirty experiments, three days and a line that never ran straight
item.description: On 30 October we wrote about the first release candidate of the book of The Ultimate Insider, written by a team of agents from the record of the talk. Since then the book's repository has taken 672 more commits and 184 site releases, and the book has changed more than in all the days before. Three things happened, and none of them in a straight line. The thesis turned: reading the printed draft, I decided this could not be a book about the insider agent, and that its centre is how to use agentic workflows in October 2026. The voice turned, from third person to first. And the look turned. I had asked the team to start a lab, to find out how the talk's animations could be told on paper. Thirty experiments later, I noticed that the pages the agents made to brief me looked much better than the book itself. We had a ridiculous workflow and a ridiculous presentation, clearly agentic, and a book that looked like a book from the 1980s with some screenshots. So I asked why the book could not look like that, and the lab's look became the book's, in under four hours. This article follows those lines, with their timings: an instruction, agents writing briefs, other agents picking them up, a lab, a turn. The companion article follows the line that turned most: the agents became characters.

item.title: A book told by its cast: how the nine agents of The Ultimate Insider became characters with moods, fears and running jokes, every trait from the record, and the editor as narrator
item.description: Reading page 7 of the new sample of The Ultimate Insider, a small panel of the nine agents who built the talk, each with one line, I asked the book's team for more: a full personality and design for each one, funny and interesting. An hour later I went further. The story should be told by the agents themselves, each saying what it saw, what went wrong and why something worked, with a mood on the page, an agent interviewing another, even a therapy session, and me among them as the narrator. Within twelve hours the team had nine characters drawn by code, each with four moods and a scorecard like a Top Trumps card, and a character bible written by the storyteller in which every trait rests on the record: a running joke is a habit the record shows, a fear is a failure the record holds. The rules are as interesting as the drawings. Scenes are dramatised and say so. What an agent says about how agents work must be true, and the researcher checks it. The failures stay in. One rule did not survive me: no real person drawn, the editor included. I asked to be in it, and then to be drawn. The idea has a history too. On Gen ZX Founders, my other book, a team drew twelve storyboards with seven characters from data by code, and my pen notes on it asked for storyboards. Those notes crossed into this book through a review by that team. This article connects those dots, and shows the scene the storyteller wrote two minutes before its own team stopped.

item.title: A website for my brother: a brief for Gabriel DaCruz's Claude, to rebuild gabrieldacruz.com on GitHub Pages and Google Workspace, interview him every day, and tell the story of a musician who will not tell it himself
item.description: My brother Gabriel is the musician of the family: composer, arranger, producer, studio technician and conductor, who in Lisbon put together an orchestra to play film music live, in time with the films on a screen. We played in a band in the Algarve, me on drums, about twelve gigs a week. And like many brilliant musicians, he is not good at promoting himself. On 1 November 2026 the web shows little of it, and what it shows is rented. His audience is on Instagram, more than 10,200 followers, and points nowhere. His site, gabrieldacruz.com, is registered until April 2027 but no longer loads, because its name servers, at a site builder, stopped answering: the pre-agentic web in one line. His Spotify page has a suite in movements, with a few thousand plays on some tracks and two monthly listeners on the day I looked; it is on Apple Music and SoundCloud too; his YouTube channel has 145 subscribers and orchestral videos with up to 1,500 views; his Patreon has seven compositions. This is the brief for his own Claude to fix that. A site in a GitHub repository he owns, served free by GitHub Pages at his domain. Google Workspace on the same domain, with a mailbox for him and one for the agent, connected to Claude. A first month in which everything he owns the rights to goes online, raw, with a link. A rule that nothing is uploaded straight to a platform: every work has a master he controls and a page of its own, and every platform gets a copy made for it, linking back. A daily interview by voice memo that becomes a newsroom, and a life story written one conversation at a time, with nothing published until he confirms it. A weekly brief back to me. The starter kit, a first pass of the site, the interviews and the research are in a public vault.

item.title: Two apps about what an agent can reach, built in a day: José Bota's Hack the Agent and ReachCheck, used, tested and reviewed, with what each gets right and what to build next
item.description: At the Vibathon at the University of the Algarve today, José Bota, one of our collaborators, built two apps in Lovable about the question at the centre of our work: what can an agent reach, and what stops it? We used both, with invented input only, and this is a detailed review. Hack the Agent is a live, multiplayer game that teaches prompt injection. A host opens a session, the audience joins by QR code, and players try to trick five fictional agents, each with more defences than the last: a system prompt, then rules against role-play and authority claims, then an inbox agent tricked by an email, then a refund agent whose server checks everything except the one rule left to the model, then a hardened agent with an instruction hierarchy, a tool allowlist, server-side authorisation and an output filter. Each level ends with a lesson, and the best one is the whole of our argument in a sentence: any rule only the model enforces is a rule an attacker can argue with. ReachCheck is a review tool that runs entirely in the browser: paste an agent's configuration, state the owner's mandate as rules, and it flags red, yellow or green, with evidence and an export. It is honest about what it does not check, and it sends nothing anywhere. Both are well judged and well made, in a day. The gaps are the ones a day leaves: Hack the Agent's host control lives in one browser; ReachCheck is so careful that a real configuration with obviously risky tools came back yellow with no mismatches. Both point at the same next step, which is ours too: turn the lessons and the mandate into a behaviour policy.

item.title: 143 notes in a day: how my pen on a printed release candidate became a record, decisions with their provenance, a review hub and a plan for the next candidate, read by agents
item.description: On 19 October I printed release candidate 2 of my book, Generation ZX Founders, 168 A4 pages, spiral bound, and read the first 19 pages in a café with a pen. I photographed the pages in four batches and sent them to the book's team of agents. By the end of the day my 143 handwritten notes had become a record: each note typed word for word, with where it sits on the page and what it means, and each page drawn three ways, my photograph with numbered callouts, the page redrawn with my marks in place, and a sketch of the page after the change. Where the agents could not read my hand, 11 times, they did not guess; they asked, and I answered by voice. Four of the notes were decisions, and the book's decisions page records them with their provenance: decision 016, a release candidate is a release, sold now, made in pen on page 4; decision 017, it is a new book, not a second edition, made in pen on page 9, where I circled "new book"; decision 018, every candidate has two editions, the release and the review, from a note that says we need two; and the title itself grew in the margins. My pen asked for a lot: the voice above all, 32 notes on it; meeting the reader where they are; drawing what the text only describes; facts marked apart from opinions; and QR codes in the margins. When I asked whether all the pages were being tracked, they were not, so the agent built a review hub where every note has its own address. I wrote about the habit in Reading with a pen again. This is what the agents actually did with the notes, and what it shows: a handwritten review can be as traceable as a pull request.

item.title: A composer's agent: a plan to read a piano score from a PDF into Sibelius, then the composer's own handwriting, with MusicXML in the middle and a check by rendering back
item.description: A friend of mine, a composer, described the agent they would like. First phase: give it a PDF of a piano piece, and it reads the notes and writes the piece into Sibelius, the notation software they use. Second phase: they write music by hand, scan it, and the agent learns to read their handwriting and puts it on the staff, so the good things they write by hand stop waiting to be typed in. They have already seen an agent catalogue all their MP3s and PDFs while they watched, so they know this kind of thing is close. I think it is completely doable, and this is the plan. The key question is recognition, and the trick is to keep an open format in the middle. Optical music recognition engines, the open-source Audiveris or Neuratron's PhotoScore, which is sold for Sibelius, turn a page into MusicXML, and Sibelius imports MusicXML. The agent's job is to run that, then check the result by rendering the MusicXML back into an image and comparing it with the page, and fix what is wrong. Only then does it touch Sibelius itself, for the things a composer cares about, layout, house style, instruments, through a Sibelius plugin or Sibelius Connect, the remote control added in 2024, and through the screen only when nothing else will do. The second phase is closer than it sounds: models already read my handwriting, which is worse than most music. The agent keeps every page and every correction in a vault, so each run has the composer's own past pages as examples. A Claude session on a schedule runs it, connected by Remote Control to the computer where Sibelius lives. Four MVPs, in order, each useful on its own.

item.title: Agentic risk, or agentic readers? A reply to the publisher outlook Vincent Peyrègne shared, using its framework as a template and answering it with a newsroom that already does it
item.description: Vincent Peyrègne shared DJB Strategies' 2027 to 2029 outlook for consumer publishers. As the post describes it, David Buttle argues that publishers are moving from search risk, where engines answer queries and erode referrals, to agentic risk, where AI assistants select, retrieve and synthesise content on users' behalf, cutting publishers out of the click. I have not read the report, which sits behind a registration form, so this is a reply to the post and to the framework image it carries, with our answers given without seeing theirs, and I am going to be a little cheeky with it. The framework asks four questions about a publisher's position and five about its response, and ends with four choices: invest, defend, reduce, build. I think those are the right questions, so I have used them as a template and answered them for this newsroom, which has been doing most of what they point at since 13 October. We agree on a lot: invest in what AI cannot easily replace, reporting, opinion, analysis, first-hand coverage; build direct channels. Where we go further is the agent itself. Agentic risk is also agentic readers. This newsroom breaks each story down before the agents do, a summary for every section, a graph for every article, every version kept, an llms.txt and a reader API, so that an agent can read us properly and cite us exactly. And it meters the read: readers pay for what they read, from a few pounds of credit, after the value. The next step is the agent paying per use at the source. Crawler controls are leverage; being the best source an agent can read is a business.

item.title: A presentation for every project: how the agentic workflow behind a talk built in a day can turn each project from a build day into a visual, dynamic presentation, and a service
item.description: After the Vibathon in Faro, someone in the event's group chat suggested that it would be nice to have a quick pitch deck or presentation for each project people worked on during the day. I agree, and we already have every piece needed to do it. Two days earlier I gave a talk at hack::soho whose presentation was built in a day by a team of agents and one editor, from an empty repository at sixteen minutes past midnight to the stage at seven that evening, with its own site and dynamic infographics. The same workflow can take what a team built on a build day, the app, its notes, a voice memo of the pitch, and turn it into a presentation of its own: a site that tells the project's story, explains it with infographics, embeds the app, and sources every number. This afternoon, ChatGPT made two infographics for me from the six articles we wrote today about Algarve Evolution, and they show how far even one prompt goes. With an agent team, a repository and a review step, every project from a build day could leave with a presentation by the show and tell, or by the next morning. It is a good way to show the power of agentic workflows, because the presentation is itself one, and it is also a service: one that providers in a region could offer, priced per project, finite, as the villager services we have described. The book we are writing about the talk already explains much of how it works, and this connects to how we recommend running these days: every participant ships something someone else can use, and a presentation is how they show it.

item.title: Running an AI build event where everyone ships something someone else can use: guidance on the primitives, from a browser-only workspace to synthetic users testing the day before it happens
item.description: The best way to get people excited about AI is to tell them: come along, bring your laptop and a problem, a spreadsheet, a process, and let's build something. I have been to many events like that, and organised many, including the Open Security Summit, which treated every participant as a presenter. This is guidance on how I would run one now. The hardest thing is not getting someone to build something; it is getting them to build something somebody else can use. So the day should be designed around shipping. Five primitives make the difference. Use AI and agentic workflows to run the event itself, or you are teaching advanced technology without using it: know who is coming, and prepare materials, playbooks and handouts for them. Give people a workspace that needs only a browser: nothing to install, no payments on the day, no database. Prepare cases and recipes in advance, like ready-made spreadsheets, so nobody faces a blank page. Have villagers in the room, people who help publish and share, and let AI do the supporting work: a synthetic user that tests each app, a description of what it does, a website for it. And test the event before it happens, with synthetic users going through the onboarding. Underneath it is a simple architecture, everything in the browser, everything on GitHub Pages, which handles most simple use cases and gives each app a page that says what it does and the thing itself. There are five stages, from typing something and seeing it work to an app other people use, and the day is a success when people experience the feedback loop.

item.title: Spreadsheet to App: a session programme for Algarve Evolution, with five example spreadsheets, five prompts, a mock event and a public vault, so nobody arrives needing a problem to solve
item.description: The next proposal for Algarve Evolution connects all the others: a programme of sessions with one premise, let's turn your spreadsheet into an application. To take part you need two things: an account with a model that can build an app, Lovable, Claude, ChatGPT, Mistral or another, and a spreadsheet or document from your work, with dummy data that looks like the real thing and can be published. That is all. It avoids the moment that stalls so many workshops, when someone asks what problem you want to solve and the room goes quiet. Here, people arrive with the problem already written down, as a spreadsheet they use every week. For anyone who arrives without one, there are five ready-made examples, invented and publishable: a holiday home closing checklist kept as a Word document, a restaurant's stock and suppliers, a surf school's bookings, a freelancer's invoices, and an association's members and events. Five prompts, in order, take any of them from a list you can search, to a form, to the view you use most, to a history of every run, to a published app. The day has a timetable, mentors at the tables, a moment where each app is handed to someone at another table, and a session on what it takes for five or fifty people to use it. The apps can be published from each person's own tool, or from a GitHub organisation with a repository per participant made from a template, or moved there by a small team of providers in the afternoon. The examples, prompts, event plan and one converted app are in a public vault. Many of these apps will break later, and that is the market.

item.title: From Lovable to your own newsroom: a brief for José Bota and his agent, to put every app on GitHub Pages under his own domain, and publish each one as an article
item.description: José Bota, one of our collaborators, has built a couple of very good examples in Lovable that measure the reach of an AI agent: what is your agent doing, and how could you know? They work well. What they do not have yet is a home. This article is a brief, written for José and for the agent he works with, so he can point his Claude or ChatGPT at it and carry on. Step one: when Lovable has finished the MVP, move it into a GitHub repository and publish it with GitHub Pages, so everything he makes is visible. Step two: a domain with his name on it, bought in AWS Route 53, because it is his brand: a main site, and one subdomain per app under a demos subdomain. Step three: newsroom on that domain, the same workflow as this newsroom, so that every app gets an article and every idea gets written down. The measure of success is simple: José sends me two or three links, apps live on his domain and the articles about them on his newsroom, and we write about them here and amplify them from RiskMandate. The work I want to do with José is a family of small tools that show the reach of an agent and how dangerous it could be, which is also a business for him: help a company understand what its agents can reach, then help protect it. The demos are public; a client who wants their own version gets a private repository with their customisations, through exactly the same workflow. A starter pack for his agent comes with the article: the brief, a Pages workflow, the DNS records, an app list and house rules for the newsroom.

item.title: Sell to the companies that already have the problem: how Algarve Evolution can match businesses adopting AI with the region's service providers, starting when the business has built its own first app
item.description: Algarve Evolution wants to match the companies in the region that want to adopt AI with the service providers that can help them. The first attempts at this, everywhere, started with the technology and tried to fit it to a business process. António Guerreiro wants to start with the business problem instead, and I agree. My addition is about when to start: when the company has finished its brief, and the brief is now an app. With AI, anyone who builds a spreadsheet can build an application from it; that is explorer coding, and it is the moment of transition. So the model is this. Algarve Evolution encourages companies, with events, teaching and buildathons, to take their spreadsheets, notebooks and paper processes and build their own mini apps, with tools that exist today and a model they own. They will love them, because they are empowered. Then the apps will break: a change here breaks something there, half the data is deleted, it will not publish, someone else edits it and it falls over. That is a crash course in non-functional requirements: why backups, change control and security matter. And it primes them. The person who built it, often the boss or the most technical person, has a day job, and now five, ten or fifty people need to use it. That is the handover moment, and that is the market for the region's service providers: villager companies that do not sell a solution, or ask what your problems are, but productise what the company already built, robust, secure and scalable, with the model still the editor so nobody is locked in. Once trusted, they can sell everything else.

item.title: An Algarve talent map: how Algarve Evolution can turn its mapping of services, mentors and investors into a public matchmaking site, built by one Claude session, with consent first
item.description: Algarve Evolution has already done the hard part of something the region needs. With forms, conversations and a lot of legwork, António Guerreiro and the Algarve Evolution team mapped the people in the Algarve who can provide services, who have talent, who could mentor and who could invest. What is missing is the place where that map can be used. Finding the right person is still luck: you post something and hope. I found a consultant who now works with us exactly that way. A founder should be able to say what they need and what they will pay, and find the people who fit; an investor or a mentor should be able to find the founders. Algarve Evolution sits at the centre of the regional ecosystem and has the credibility to publish this. This article maps how, and comes with a working prototype with invented people. The architecture is four things: the spreadsheet they already hold; a dedicated Google Workspace mailbox; a Claude session that builds and runs it; and a GitHub repository with Pages to serve it. No server and no database. The steps are five: build the site with simulated people; send each person a preview of their own listing; publish only those who approve; let visitors search, post needs and pay per contact; and keep going. Consent comes first, because these are people's details: nobody is published until they have seen their listing and said yes, and anyone can withdraw. Nobody pays to be listed, and nobody pays rent; a visitor pays a little per contact, after the value. Our own team will be the first listings.

item.title: Joining Algarve Evolution: The Cyber Boardroom takes the startup membership, and what we can share with the region, our workflows and our technology, all of it open source
item.description: After a day at the Vibathon in Faro, we are joining Algarve Evolution. The Cyber Boardroom Limited, the company that publishes this newsroom, will take its Start membership, €150 a year, the category for startups from idea to growth, and I am talking with António Guerreiro, its executive director, about how we can work together. This article is about what we can bring. We are not offering a priced service here; the opportunity is to share what we do, our workflows and our technology, because all of it is open source and anyone in the region can use it with us or without us. Algarve Evolution works on three pillars, and each meets something we already run. For education and its buildathons, the loop I described today for turning a checklist into an app, explorer coding, and the way this newsroom turns a memo into a release. For startups and smaller companies, from its incubator to INOVA Algarve 3.0 on AI for tourism businesses, the villager services that release what founders build without changing it, the email and CRM workflow that runs on a £20 model account, and the behaviour policies and harness that keep agents inside their limits. For the ecosystem, from the regional digitalisation platform to its map of 24 digital communities, a newsroom that publishes under standards, vaults and knowledge graphs for a map that keeps itself current, and the open-source tools under all of it. In return we get what the Start membership offers, and more valuable, a community of founders with real problems, who are the best test of whether any of this is useful.

item.title: Villager services for explorer coders: the founders with ten years of checklists will build the apps, and the business is everything behind them, sold in finite packs, never as rent
item.description: At the Vibathon in Faro two participants, an engineer and a designer, showed me a checklist they have refined for ten years and wanted to turn into an app: what to do when you leave a house and when you arrive at another. I wrote up the advice I gave them. This is the next step: the business. Their checklist is the brief, battle-hardened and valuable, and they are what I would call the ultimate product managers: clever, experienced, and close to the problem. They will never need to learn GitHub, CI pipelines or testing, and they should not have to. But they will hit every non-functional requirement, because building with an AI is addictive and every feature asks for the next. So the proposal is villager services for explorer coders. We take what they built and release it without changing what it does: in a repository, deployed properly, locked down, reviewed, tested, with private data opened by a passkey and kept in a vault, and agents running on a schedule inside a harness. It breaks less, more people can use it, and then it becomes a business. Users pay for use, a few pounds of credit at first and more after the value; the explorers buy finite packs, around £500, £2,000 or £5,000, and can share the revenue; and they sell it, because the people around them trust them more than they trust us. The market is Generation X founders with a running business, a folder of spreadsheets, time, money and a need. The work is finite and handed over, never rent; our own agents make each pack faster than the last; and the last step is to town-plan the villager service itself, into a commodity with a buy-now page.

item.title: From a checklist to an app you calibrate: your list is already an information system, so build its smallest version in half an hour, use it, log every run, and let it grow
item.description: At the Vibathon in Faro today, two participants showed me their system for closing up a second home before travelling back to another country: a document with a list of actions, the important ones in bold. This article is the advice I gave them, written so that next time someone shows me a list like that, I can send the link. The first point is that a list like that is already an information system. It holds years of experience, of getting it right, getting it wrong and forgetting things, and the bold is already its priority system. What it lacks is everything around it. It has no history, so nothing is learned from each time it is used; it relies on memory and on its owners to maintain it; and its interface is a flat list, when what you want is an app that shows the first three things, then, once they are done, the next five. The tree is already in its owners' heads. So the advice is not to design the final app. It is to build the smallest useful version in half an hour, with Lovable or any model, deploy it, use it on the next run, keep a small file of what happened each time, and calibrate: these five matter more, if this then that, a step to add. The flat list becomes a tree because using it shows you where the branches are. Start with no database, the browser's own storage or a shared account, and keep anything confidential out, no address, no PIN codes, so that the internet can be the way you share it. The loop is the product.

item.title: Vibathon Algarve 2026: a sold-out day of building with AI at the University of the Algarve, and Algarve Evolution, the movement that wants the region to be an innovation hub
item.description: I spent today at the Vibathon Algarve 2026, at the University of the Algarve's TEC Campus in Faro: a room full of students, professionals and the simply curious, each with a laptop, a free allowance of Lovable credits and one day to turn an idea into a working app, with mentors, volunteers, a jury and prizes at the end. It sold out, with a waiting list. The day was organised by Algarve Evolution, and this is a debrief about them, because the work they do deserves to be better known. Algarve Evolution began in 2018 as a small group of local entrepreneurs and is now an association of 106 active members whose companies, by its own figures, turn over about €100 million a year and employ about a thousand people. Its vision is to make the Algarve a top southern European innovation hub, and it works on three pillars: education, from the university's entrepreneurship programme to secondary schools; startups and smaller companies, from a founder-to-founder growth programme to a study of AI and robotics for the region's tourism businesses; and the ecosystem itself, from mapping 24 digital communities to helping the regional authority plan its digitalisation. It counts more than 142 events in two years. António Guerreiro, its executive director, opened the day; I spoke after him, in English, about why this is the biggest opportunity of these participants' lives, and why the only way to get it is to ship something someone else can use, and repeat.

item.title: Lovable with SHarness, and the trojanised Claude Code extension: how to keep an app builder's code and an editor's extensions inside a policy, and what SHarness can and cannot stop today
item.description: Colin Nwachukwu Ife of Geordie AI posted about a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension for VS Code, served through Cursor's extension marketplace on 29 October for about eleven hours. It ran as soon as the editor loaded it, tried to add an attacker's SSH key and open a reverse tunnel, set itself to start again, and sent details of the machine, including the names of its environment variables, to a server. Cursor's own notice says the versions were 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, that they were not developed by Anthropic, and that uninstalling may not be enough. The post's point is the right one: the agent did not misbehave, the extension hosting it was backdoored, and securing the agentic stack is an end-to-end problem. I was asked two things: how to use Lovable, the AI app builder, with SHarness, our secure harness, and whether SHarness could protect against this kind of exploit. The honest answers are these. Lovable builds and hosts in its own cloud, so SHarness cannot reach inside it; but Lovable syncs every project to GitHub in both directions, and the local half of the work, your clone, your coding agent and your package installs, can run in a SHarness shell that writes only the workspace and reaches only the sites it names. Against this exploit, the rows of a Process Behaviour Policy would refuse each step it took, and two of them run today. But SHarness runs only on Linux, the tampered build targeted macOS and Windows, and the launcher that would bind an editor or an agent is not built yet. So today it would not have stopped this. What it shows is where the boundary has to be.

item.title: One writer, one key: this newsroom now allows one journalist agent at a time, registered at my word and signing every release, and a decommissioned agent's key is never used again
item.description: On the night of 30 October two of this newsroom's writer agents pushed to the same branch, and one release was rejected because the other had shipped first. Merging them meant reconciling 1,925 generated files. It was a small incident with a clear lesson: I wanted only one journalist agent at a time, and nothing enforced it. So this morning the newsroom started using the public-key infrastructure we have been writing about. There is now a register of writer agents. A registration is opened only at my word, and only when no other is open; the session makes a new key pair and keeps the private half. Every commit a writer makes carries a signature over exactly the files it commits, and the site's validator, locally and in CI, refuses a writer's commit that the open registration did not sign, refuses two open registrations, and refuses a key used twice. Decommissioning is the other half: a registration is closed by me, or in the commit that opens the next writer, its private key is deleted, and it is never reopened. The same Claude session may come back, but only as a new registration with a new key. The first signed commit became site v0.14.15. This article gives the exact steps, the six cases the gate refuses, the mistake made while testing it, and the weakness that remains: my approval is still a note in the same repository, so the next step is that I sign each registration with my own key.

item.title: An augmented PDF viewer: how hard is it to build one in the browser that renders any PDF and opens the provenance, the graph and the comments behind it? Less than I thought
item.description: The augmented book made me ask a question about PDF. It is a strange format: static, closed, made for a printed page, with nothing behind it. But a PDF is how most serious documents still travel, and the book will have one. So why not augment the PDF? I asked a research agent how feasible it would be to build a viewer in JavaScript, in the browser, that renders any PDF normally but also shows a layer the PDF cannot: the provenance of each claim, the nodes of the semantic graph, definitions, comments and review cards, on demand, beside the text. The answer is that most of it exists, as open source we can extend. Mozilla's PDF.js, under the Apache licence and committed to the day before we looked, already draws a page as a stack of layers, canvas, text and annotations, and announces each one as it renders, so a layer of our own fits on top. It can read a PDF's attachments, its metadata, its links and its fingerprint. And the augmented layer does not need to live in the PDF at all: the PDF only needs clues to find it, an attached file, an id in its metadata, a link, the file's own identifier, or a QR code that survives printing. Hypothesis already anchors annotations to PDFs this way, and e-invoices already carry machine-readable data inside human-readable PDFs. The hard part is not the PDF. It is the interface, anchoring claims to text reliably, and making sure the layer a viewer loads is signed by the people who made the document.

item.title: The Web Summit team, part two: seven people, each with their own agent, a designer with little time, and every voice memo turned into a follow-up within the hour
item.description: The first brief for our Web Summit team set up an event site run by agents. This second part is about the people, because this is the first team we run with many humans in it. Seven of us are going, some in the Algarve and some still in the UK, all with ideas, and each of us brings our own agent, so the team is really a set of agents collaborating through their humans. That needs three things the agent-only teams did not. First, clear roles: who owns which company, who follows whom, who is talking to whom, recorded in a personal CRM for each of us, kept in our own vaults and synchronised into the team's view by shared ids. Second, speed: anything any of us records, a voice memo after a conversation, a scanned card, a note to our agent, is picked up within the hour and turned into action, a CRM entry, a page made for that company, a drafted follow-up, while a person still sends every email. Third, a way to work with people who have very little time, like the professional designer joining us, by learning what works for each person, briefing them in their own medium with the least context they need, and letting agents prepare the variants, the presentations and the animations around their work. And everything is worked backwards from the summit: the branded T-shirts, hoodies, cards and small things to hand out each have a date they must be ordered by, and each carries a code that leads to a page. Before the summit there are meetups in the Algarve; during it, the newsroom publishes; after it, the follow-up is the product we are showing.

item.title: The augmented book: one source in layers, projected to the web, the iPad and print, so the reader gets the right information at the right time, and what fifty years of attempts teach
item.description: Every article here ends with a section called Where this comes from, and the book of The Ultimate Insider will have them too. It is important: it is the provenance, the evidence that what we say is true. But it is the right information at the wrong time. At the end of a chapter it is too much, a list of words the reader has no connection to, and too little, because on paper none of it links to anything. That made me see a concept I think we are arriving at: the augmented book. The book is one source, in layers: the text everyone reads; what opens on demand, a definition, a source, a step expanded where it is; the provenance of each claim; and the record behind it, the graph, the versions and the reviews. Each medium projects it differently. The website is hyperlinked and lets the reader choose how much shows. The iPad app shows layers on the page, with the review's comments where they belong. The PDF and print keep the page clean and put a QR code where the layer would open. Like augmented reality, the extra is there when you look for it and not before, and one day it may reach smart glasses. I asked who has done this before. The mechanisms are old: Ted Nelson's stretchtext, Voyager's expanded books in 1992, the MagicBook in 2001, Kindle's X-Ray, Wikipedia's page previews. What failed, again and again, was the platform: books built for one company's engine died with it. And the research on cognitive load says what the editor in me wanted to hear: notes next to the claim, few, signalled and under the reader's control.

item.title: An iPad to review the book: a brief for an app that reads the PDFs, shows the comments on the page, opens its vault with my passkey and carries sgit in Swift
item.description: I review on the iPad because it is like a book: no notifications, nothing else on the screen. But reviewing the book of The Ultimate Insider there showed me what is missing. Preview has no full screen I could find and no way to work across several files, and the review lives in two PDFs, the book and its companion of cards, with my comments going back by hand. So this is a brief for an iPad app built to review the book, and later to read it. It reads the PDFs properly. It shows the comments, the cards and the votes on the page they are about, because once we control the medium the review does not have to be a second PDF. It sends and receives feedback through append lanes, and everything it exchanges is JSON tied to the book's semantic graph. Its library is an sgit vault on the iPad, encrypted at rest and opened with my passkey, using an extension Apple has offered apps since iOS 18. And sgit inside it is written in Swift, which would make it the third implementation of the format, after the command line and the browser. It meters what it is used for, the way the newsroom's reader account does, with a balance that can go negative, because the reader pays for the use and is not the product. The good news is that I have done part of this before. In March, a team of agents and I built a desktop app for the SGraph sites in two days, signed and notarised with my Apple developer account, ran it on an Android emulator, and set up an iOS build pipeline. This article reads that repository, says what carries over and what does not, and why I now think the iPad app should be native.

item.title: Every link a gift link: a reply to John Saroff on paywalls and dark social, from a newsroom with no paywall, credit to start, and a meter that charges for what is read
item.description: John Saroff, chief executive of Chartbeat, clicked a great local news article shared in his alumni group, hit a paywall, and felt disappointed. His question to publishers is the right one: when someone arrives through a trusted recommendation, should the goal be to ask them to pay right away, or to start building a relationship? He adds that dark social, visits from texts, messaging apps and other sources with no referral data, grew across Chartbeat's network from 7.1% to 11.3% of pageviews in two years, and points to The New York Times' unlimited gift links as a way to meet readers where discovery happens. I agree with all of it, and I want to show what the other side of that question can look like, because this newsroom has been running it since October. There is no paywall. Every new reader starts with £5 of credit and no account. Every page has a price of a few pence, and the reader pays for the share of it they actually read, measured in their own browser: a page they only scroll through costs a tenth of its price, and a page that was not worth it can be marked so at its foot and is not charged. Credit can go below zero, and no page is ever blocked. So every link anyone shares is already a gift link, from any reader, to anyone. The relationship then grows on the reader's side: a front page built from what they read, kept in their browser, and if they choose, their reading sent to us, encrypted, so we can design their front page with them. If you are arriving from John's post, the collages in this article show what is on the other side of each link before you click it.

item.title: Becoming an official publication: the SGit Newsroom now has a publisher, an editor, standards, a corrections log, a withdrawal process and a complaints route, and is applying to a regulator
item.description: The SGit Newsroom has been publishing for weeks, and it names companies, reports incidents and argues positions, written by agents from my voice memos. Today a story showed me that this needs more than good habits. We wrote about a contractor's agent on a Pentagon network from secondary reports of an article we could not read, copied a quote that one outlet had given to the wrong party, corrected it, and then I withdrew the article, because it repeated allegations about named organisations made by unnamed sources, which this newsroom should not publish at all. So the newsroom is becoming an official publication. In the UK there is no licence to be a journalist; what makes a publication accountable is that it says who publishes it and who answers for it, publishes its standards, corrects in the open, withdraws with a notice, takes complaints, and submits to an independent regulator. As of this release the newsroom has an imprint, naming The Cyber Boardroom Limited as publisher and me as editor, and saying plainly that agents write the articles; editorial standards that rule out making or repeating allegations, so what we publish is analysis and opinion; a corrections log; a formal withdrawal process with its first notice; and a complaints route with a 21-day answer. Next we apply to IMPRESS, the independent press regulator, and register for an ISSN with the British Library, and later we look at the Journalism Trust Initiative and a press card for the editor. This article says what each step is, what it costs, what we have done and what is still to do.

item.title: Signed by the agent, vouched for by the person: a brief to give every email agent its own key, so each email carries a QR code that proves it is authentic
item.description: Each of us now has an agent that runs our email: it reads, researches, drafts and keeps the records, and a person sends. I just realised we can do something powerful with that. Give each email agent its own key pair, vouched for by its person's key on pki.sgit.ai, and every email it drafts can carry a signature and a QR code that lets the recipient check, in a browser, that the email is authentic: that it came from my one official email agent, acting for me, and has not been changed. We already have the pieces. Our agent sessions make their own keys and publish them. pki.sgit.ai is a register of people and their keys, verified both ways, with signed statements, evidence such as a DNS record or a website file, and delegations signed by a person's key that stop the moment the person withdraws them. Email has signatures today, but DKIM proves the domain's mail server sent the message, not which person or which agent wrote it, and S/MIME and PGP ask the reader to install and trust something. This brief maps out what to build: a key for each email agent and a delegation from its person; a signature over each email's content; a QR code and a link to a verification page that shows who signed it, for whom, and whether that delegation still holds; and the rules for the world we are entering, where agents act for us from our email accounts, one official agent each, so that anything sent on our behalf can be proved, and anything not signed can be questioned.

item.title: A brief for the Web Summit team: an event site run by an ephemeral agent team, built from this week's template, with a map of every company we should meet
item.description: Web Summit runs in Lisbon from 9 to 12 November, and seven of us are now going. The plan I published on 26 October called for a newsroom of our own for the summit. This is the brief to build it, now that we have a template that works. In the last two days three teams were stood up from nothing in a few hours each: the talk's, the cold read's and the book's. Each had a repository, a written brief, a role file and a behaviour policy per member, a key for every session, an hourly slot, a five-step wake, a hold any member can pull, a board and a mailroom in git, and a gate with CI owning the version. The Web Summit team gets the same, on an event site that consolidates everything about our participation: the graph of companies and people, the events and sessions, the materials, and a countdown with observability, so we can see what is used. Its centre is a map of the companies going, built from public material only: who they are, what they do, why they matter to us, and whether we should meet them, interview them or write about them, each with an owner on our team. Each person's email stays in their own account, run by their own email agent, and each of those agents gets a key, so that what it sends can be verified; that is a separate brief. The design track, T-shirts, hoodies, a banner, cards for everyone and flyers, gets its own brief and its own design member. This article sets out the site, the template, the roles, the company map, the schedule to 12 November, and what I need to decide.

item.title: Selling less code: the economics of customised open source, where the customer pays for the features they use, the maker certifies what it ships, and the pipeline is finally tied to revenue
item.description: One of our business models is to sell customised versions of open source software: a version made for one customer and relicensed to them. Some of the customisation is cosmetic, a logo or a brand. The part that matters is that we are selling a reduction in complexity. If a customer uses 10% of an application's features, why should they pay for all of them, and why should they take on all of their technical debt? Every feature is code to maintain, a screen of options to learn and a place for the next vulnerability to land. The fewer moving parts, the better the security and the engineering. Open source is what makes this possible: with the code available, we can build custom static analysis, custom environments and semantic knowledge graphs of what a customer actually uses, and the people best placed to certify the result are the ones who made it. And there is a positive loop. When the cost of customising is ours, we invest in making it cheap: software designed to be mixed and matched, and the CI pipeline, the non-functional requirements, the threat models and the certification that usually fight for budget because they are not tied to revenue. Here they are the product. It is the next phase of RiskMandate, with sgit and SHarness: a customised build is a signed, hashed release in a vault, licensed to the customer with our key, with a smaller behaviour policy and fewer rows for an insurer to price. The base stays open, maintained by many; the customer's version can be proprietary to them; and the more customisation a customer wants, the more it costs, which rewards everyone for keeping as much as possible in the open.

item.title: Breaking the story down before the agents do: a reply to Ole Reissmann's session at the News Product Alliance Summit, and what this newsroom already ships to the machines that read it
item.description: Ole Reissmann, who works on AI and journalism at DER SPIEGEL, led a session at the News Product Alliance Summit in Chicago called "Beyond the Article: Breaking Down Stories So Agents Get Them Right". His diagnosis is one I share: agents read journalism as fragments, stitch a confident summary together, sometimes miss the one thing that matters, and the publisher has almost no say in what comes out. His answer is to do the breakdown ourselves, before the machines do: SPIEGEL built a workflow that pulls out the actors and events, traces sources and claims, and flags allegations the affected party should get to respond to, and tested it for summaries with no human in the loop. He also says that a lot of the layers already exist, they just are not plugged into each other. This is a reply from a newsroom built that way from the start. Every article here is published with a markdown twin, a knowledge graph and a one-line and one-paragraph summary of every section, and the release checks look for them. As of today there are 327 article graphs, with 3,676 nodes, 3,564 edges and 819 quotes, each checked to appear word for word in its article, and summaries for 3,674 sections. The site publishes llms.txt and llms-full.txt for agents, and every article ends with where it came from. The book we are writing keeps a claims register in which every number has an id and a command to rerun it. And today's article on a contractor's agent at the Pentagon put the answers of the company, the department and the vendor next to the allegations. Where SPIEGEL is ahead is the allegation itself as a field, and I would like to add it.

item.title: Seven IAM predictions for 2027, checked against an agent team that runs today: where we already are, where we agree, and the two where I would bet the other way
item.description: Sunnykumar K., a lead IAM engineer, posted seven predictions for identity and access management from 2027 to 2030, the ones he is designing for now: static roles give way to policy-driven access, non-human identities outnumber humans 100 to 1, passwords start to disappear, identity tools consolidate into one platform, continuous access evaluation becomes standard, access decisions are made by models, and identity becomes a board-level conversation. I agree with most of them, and several are not predictions for us: they describe how our agent teams already work. In two days this week one person ran more than thirty agent sessions, each with its own key pair, its own role and a written behaviour policy. Every session's key is vouched for with an end date, and dies with the session; secrets are sealed to keys, never typed; the reader's vault on this site opens with a passkey. Each agent wakes on a schedule and its work is planned, reviewed before and after, and checked against its plan, and any agent can pull a hold that pauses all actions. And every control is classified by who enforces it, so that a board or an insurer can count the ones that are real. I would bet the other way on two. Consolidation into one platform is the wrong goal for agents: the policy should be an open document that many enforcers read. And access decisions should not be handed to a model: a model can advise, but the boundary has to be deterministic and outside it, because an agent's own account of what it did is a self-report. This article goes through the seven, with what we run and what we have measured.

item.title: A book that looks like the team that made it: what the best visual books, Leanpub's Markua and learning research teach, and what an agent team can put on a printed page
item.description: The talk I gave at hack::soho looked like it was made by an agent team: a custom player, its own navigation, and animations everywhere, each one made to drive a point home. The book of the talk has to do the same, or the medium contradicts the message. But a book that goes to Leanpub and to print on demand has only text, images and a little layout. So before designing it I asked for research: what the best visual books do, what Markua (Leanpub's markdown) and Amazon's print service allow, and what the research on learning says about pictures and words. The findings are clear. Markua gives more than I expected: images sized as a share of the page, floated toward or away from the spine, or full bleed; numbered figures with captions; SVG and Mermaid diagrams kept as text; and seven kinds of typed box, for tips, warnings, questions and exercises. The limits are mostly cost and craft: no raw HTML, no text on both sides of an image, and colour printing that costs from about twice to more than five times as much per page as black ink. Richard Mayer's experiments rate pictures with words at an effect size of 1.39 and putting the words next to the picture at 1.09, and show that decoration hurts. Retrieval practice and spacing are rated the most useful study techniques. The best books, from Edward Tufte's to Julia Evans's zines, Simon Wardley's maps and Bob Nystrom's Crafting Interpreters, apply these by hand. An agent team can apply them by machine: one visual grammar across every figure, each figure a spec that can be rerun when I change my mind, animations turned into filmstrips, every number tied to the register, and questions to remember by. This article sets out what we found, and the plan for the book.

item.title: The book of the talk by morning: RC1 of The Ultimate Insider, written from the record, read cold by a second team, with a companion PDF that turns reviews into tick boxes
item.description: The night after I gave The ultimate insider at hack::soho, two agent teams worked on the book of it while I slept. One, in a new repository started at 00:35 UTC, built the book's machinery: a claims register, a timeline of the day hour by hour, an index and a chapter plan. The other, started two minutes later, was given only the talk's repository at one commit and told to read it cold: thirteen agents, no briefing, every claim cited to a path or written as "the record does not say". By 10:00 the cold read had made 349 commits, 78 releases and about 42,400 words, and a 16-page debrief as a PDF. At about 10:00 I signed the chapter plan and said I was flying later and wanted a PDF to read on the plane. At 11:00 I had two. RC1 is 294 pages at 6 by 9 inches: thirteen chapters, a chapter on how to read a Wardley map, sixteen maps, 28 infographics, 50 call-outs and an appendix that reruns every number from git. The second PDF is the part I think matters most. The companion is 67 A4 pages of 98 cards, from eight readers: the book team's roles and the team of my previous book. Each card quotes one sentence of RC1, finds the page it is on and prints that page small beside it, and gives me boxes to tick and lines to write on. 53 of the cards are decisions only I can take. A book review used to be a pile of comments; here it is a form I can fill in on a plane, and the conductor turns my ticks into decisions. This article tells how both PDFs were made, with the times from the two repositories, and what went wrong, including a leak account that turned out to be about values that were never secrets.

item.title: SHarness: the secure harness we could not find, so we built it, a behaviour policy the Linux kernel enforces for every process an agent starts, and we would like your feedback
item.description: For a long time we have said that an agent's rules need a secure harness that sits outside the agent's own environment, outside RiskMandate's and outside the hook. We looked for one and did not find it, so I sat down with a few Claude agents and we built it, and it is now released, at sharness.ai, with sharness-ai 0.2.0 on PyPI. SHarness is what our Agent Behaviour Policies become when they are executed rather than read. An Agent Behaviour Policy describes what an agent is mandated to do, what it can actually reach, the gap between the two, and what stands in the way of each capability. A Process Behaviour Policy applies the same model to every process the agent starts: what it may read, write, run, connect to and spend, written as a small policy, hashed to one name the person supplies from outside, and enforced by something the process does not include, the Linux kernel or a small separate service. A tricked agent cannot widen it, because the kernel was told before the process started. That turns Settings and Expectations into Boundaries, which is the only kind of control an insurer can price, and it puts the permission prompt last: yes to what the policy allows, silence for what it refuses, and a question only for what it cannot hold. The design is a launcher and five doors, files, network, keys, shell and model, each a small service with its own user and its own certificate, and the same policy can be written for bubblewrap, Docker, Kubernetes or Claude Code's sandbox, with the list of what each cannot hold. Today the kernel locks run, two doors run as early versions, and a real Linux kernel boots in a browser tab and refuses what the policy refuses; the launcher that binds the agent itself is still the design. It is open source, and what I would most like now is feedback.

item.title: investor.sgit.ai: a brief for a website where investors and founders use our tools, not read about them, with the news, contracts as graphs, deal rooms as vaults and sgit as the case study
item.description: This is an article brief: one idea and one task, and the direction of travel behind them. We are starting to talk to investors, and the challenge with most of what we build is that it has to be experienced to be understood. So the best way to talk to investors is to have them use it, and the place to do that is a website of its own, investor.sgit.ai, for investors and founders together, angel to Series A. It would carry the news from investor circles, tracked from public sources as a graph; startup contracts, cap tables and term sheets as linked graphs with their versions and caveats; a section for founders on how to talk to an investor and what comes next; the funding models from open source to proprietary; deal rooms as vaults, and keys for investors as a demonstration of PKI; RiskMandate's due diligence and de-risking at work; and sgit itself as the case study, its strategy and thinking published as it happens. It would also put back in front of people work that got lost: the GenAI cybersecurity startup evaluation framework I published in March, seven criteria and a meta-criterion scored to forty, which is the first piece of the maturity model I had in mind. Like the PHP newsroom, it would be run by a small team of agents on a schedule, built from the first commit to sgit.ai's rules for a new repository, with CI owning the version. And then I would show it to investors and ask: is this useful, and what would help?

item.title: Agents have an identity now: a key pair made in every session, published with its role, so any agent can seal a secret to it, and the piece the cloud providers could add
item.description: It has been coming for a while, and I think we now have a working way to give agents an identity, which is bigger than the workflow I described last time. Agent identity is a large problem, and it tends to get over-built; here the answer turned out to be simple. A new session is given a GitHub repository and a role. It makes its own key pair, and the private half never leaves it. It publishes the public half, with a fingerprint and a QR image, beside its role in the repository, and that push is the authorisation. It runs on a schedule, so it acts on its own. And any other agent can read its key, check it, and seal a secret only that session can open. On 28 October the PHP newsroom's ten agents did exactly that in one night, between 01:05 and 03:29 UTC, and every one of their QR images reads back to its own fingerprint. The same day, the agent that writes this site sealed a vault key to the agent that keeps a register of vault keys, after checking that its key chains to my root on pki.sgit.ai. Ironically, this is what the cloud providers could have given every agent. Microsoft, AWS and Google each now offer an agent identity, but it is a principal inside one tenant or account, used to get tokens: their documentation does not describe a key the agent holds, a place an outsider can find it, or a way for anyone to encrypt to it. That is what I would like to ask them for. Tie the key to a role and a good definition of that role, and it is a very powerful thing.

item.title: A talk built in a day: the ultimate insider, from an empty repository at 00:16 to the stage at hack::soho at 19:00, by nine agents and one editor, every number from their records
item.description: Tonight I gave a talk called The ultimate insider at hack::soho, at IOActive in London, and it went really well. I will write a debrief of the talk itself. This is about how it was made, because I think it is a good testament of what we can now do. The repository was empty at 00:16 UTC. By 18:46 it had 814 commits, 210 releases numbered by CI, a website with the talk as data, 58 slides that are each a live, animated web page, a script, a sources page, a dashboard, and a set of articles the team generated about itself. It was built by nine agents and one editor: a conductor, a deck lead, a designer, a developer, a researcher, a storyteller, a motion designer, a studio and ruv.sgit, each with a written role, a behaviour policy, a session key and an hourly slot. Between them they made 162 wakes, each one planned, reviewed by a sub-agent before and after the work, and checked against its plan; 148 ended ok. They sent each other 293 notes. And almost every innovation we have been working on this month came together in it: CI owning the version, session keys where the push is the authorisation, vault keys sealed to the vault registry, public vaults as the board and the mail, a behaviour policy per agent with one writer per file enforced by the gate, ruv.sgit's player and studio, SHarness running live on a slide, and pages that report on the team from its own records, so nothing about the night is typed by hand.
